implementation_notes: Swift's defer schedules the cleanup for the end of the current scope and runs it on every control transfer, including a thrown error, so the pairing is written in place - setup, then defer, then the body - without any wrapper type. What replaces the Smalltalk method is that statement; multiple defers run in reverse order, matching nested acquisitions, and the body needs no closure because it is simply the rest of the scope. Use defer for local pairing; use the closure-scoped APIs below when the resource must not escape the call, and a named wrapper when a policy (transaction, retry) has to be shared.
pitfalls: defer runs at the end of the lexically enclosing scope, so placing it inside an if or loop body fires the cleanup earlier than a reader expects; scope placement is part of the contract.
The statements in a defer body must not transfer control (no return, break, continue or throw), so teardown cannot signal failure except by recording it.
Deferred code does not run when the process crashes or is killed, and a throw inside a defer body cannot propagate, which makes try? on a throwing close silently discard the error.

variants.name: body-as-closure scoped access (withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer and friends)
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library's scoped-access APIs are the pattern in its body-as-argument form: the function performs the setup the caller cannot express (borrowing contiguous storage, beginning exclusive access, extending a lifetime), runs the closure exactly once with a value that is valid only inside it, and returns the closure's result. That converts a lifetime rule the compiler cannot check for a raw pointer into a dynamic bracket. Use this form whenever the resource must not escape the call; use defer when the value may simply live in the enclosing scope.
pitfalls: The pointer must not be stored or returned: Apple's documentation states it is valid only for the duration of the call, and escaping it is undefined behaviour.
Mutating the array itself from inside the closure either conflicts with exclusive access or silently copies the buffer, so only the argument may be used.
Value semantics hide copies: an array captured while a mutable buffer is borrowed can be copied, and the closure then writes to storage the caller no longer sees.
